cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf (Camellia sinensis var. assamica), old seed-grown gardens of the Manzhuang and Manlin villages
processing: Raw pu-erh: pan-fired, hand-rolled and sun-dried maocha pressed into cakes; the thick leaf is rolled a little more firmly than in Yiwu.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to April) for the main harvest; autumn tea is sold more cheaply.
appearance_dry: Large, thick, dark twisted leaves with plenty of silver buds, pressed into a medium cake.
appearance_wet: Big, thick, leathery olive-green leaves, more robust than Yibang's small leaf next door.
taste_profile: Heavier than its neighbours: honey and dried flowers, a clear but smooth bitterness, a thick full body, a long sweet finish and a warming depth that makes it the most 'Menghai-like' of the six ancient mountains.

brewing.notes: Rinse once. Thick leaf; give the first steep a little time to open, then keep them short. It holds up well in a clay pot.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year and village (Manzhuang, Manlin and the surrounding hamlets), as boutique cakes and maocha since the mid-2000s revival of the six ancient mountains. Young (1–3 years) it is full and slightly bitter; it ages very well across the 5–15-year window into thick honeyed tea, and because it was blended anonymously before that, aged Manzhuan under its own name is rare. Supply is 2005–2025, dry-stored, and prices sit between Yibang and Yiwu for genuine old-tree tea.
description:
Manzhuan is one of the six ancient tea mountains of Xishuangbanna, lying between Yibang and Yiwu in Xiangming township, Mengla County, and it kept more of its old gardens through the twentieth century than Yibang, Gedeng or Mangzhi did. The tea is the big-bodied member of the family: where Yibang is fine and perfumed, Manzhuan is thick, honeyed and strong.

The gardens are seed-grown large-leaf trees around the villages of Manzhuang and Manlin at roughly 1,100–1,400 m, in a landscape of mixed forest and newer plantings. Processing is standard sheng, with a slightly firmer roll than the Yiwu habit, and the maocha looks broad and sturdy.

In the cup, Manzhuan gives honey and dried flowers, a clear bitterness that stays smooth rather than sharp, a thick full body and a long sweet finish with a warming, almost woody depth; it is the closest the Mengla side gets to a Menghai tea. It ages handsomely, filling out rather than fading, and it is a sensible cake to buy young and sit on.

Sold by spring year and village, usually as boutique cakes, at prices between Yibang and Yiwu. Because it sits next to Yiwu, some Manzhuan leaf is sold as Yiwu and some lesser leaf is sold as Manzhuan; the thick broad leaf and the heavier body are the giveaway. It is still a somewhat undervalued name, which is good news for the buyer.

For a six-mountains flight, drink Yibang for fragrance, Manzhuan for body and Youle for bite.
history:
Manzhuan is counted among the six ancient tea mountains of Xishuangbanna, on the Mengla side of the Lancang river. Its tea is known mainly through that group rather than under a story of its own.

Little is documented about Manzhuan as a separate named tea. Old leaf from the area was generally sold without the mountain's name, and cakes labelled by mountain and village are a recent habit of the boutique market.
